q-idiom-meaning.label: Meaning of an idiom
q-idiom-meaning.summary: An idiom in inverted commas; pick the option that gives its meaning.

rules.text: An idiom means something different from its words put together. Never choose the option that restates the literal picture.
rules.ok: Spill the beans = reveal a secret.
rules.bad: Spill the beans = drop some beans.

rules.text: Idioms cluster by feeling: trouble, anger, secrecy, ease, effort, luck, haste. Decide the feeling from the sentence, then match the option with that feeling.
rules.ok: 'in hot water' and 'on thin ice' both say trouble or risk.
rules.bad: Choosing an effort meaning for 'in hot water'.

q-idiom-meaning.cue: 'Select the most appropriate meaning of the idiom/phrase' with the idiom in inverted commas. Four to five per paper in total; three appeared in the three 12 Sep 2025 papers.
q-idiom-meaning.standard: Recall the meaning as a unit, then match it. If you do not know it, work out the feeling the idiom carries (good, bad, secret, effort, anger) from the sentence it came from.
q-idiom-meaning.fast: Drop any option that is the literal reading, then match the remaining ones by feeling.
q-idiom-meaning.eliminate: Other idioms' meanings are usually the wrong options; if you recognise one of them as belonging to a different idiom, cross it out.
traps: The literal meaning is nearly always listed as bait.
The meaning of a similar-sounding idiom is the second common trap.
Do not pick an option only because it contains a word from the idiom.

pyqs.text: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: At sixes and sevens
options: A dilemma between two evils
A free and fair decision
In complete confusion
A selection made under duress
pyqs.why: At sixes and sevens describes disorder or confusion, as when nobody knows who is doing what.

a.note: A choice between two evils is a dilemma ('between a rock and a hard place'), not confusion; the numbers six and seven tempt one to think of 'two'.

b.note: A free and fair decision is about choice, not disorder.

d.note: A forced selection is about pressure, not about things being in a muddle.

pyqs.trick: Think 'a mess': sixes and sevens is a muddle, never a choice.

pyqs.text: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: Leave no stone unturned
options: To keep shifting from one place to another repeatedly
To make every possible effort to achieve a goal
To remain quiet as a form of protest
To obey someone without questioning
pyqs.why: To leave no stone unturned is to search or try in every way, so that nothing is missed.

a.note: This reads 'stone' and 'turning' as movement; the idiom is about completeness of effort, not travel.

c.note: Staying quiet in protest has no link to effort or searching.

d.note: Obeying without questioning is about submission, not effort.

pyqs.trick: 'No stone left' means everything was tried: effort, not travel.

pyqs.text: Choose the correct meaning of idiom: Blow a fuse
options: To slip away quietly
To vanish suddenly
To become suddenly angry
To manage a situation smartly
pyqs.why: When a fuse blows, the circuit breaks suddenly; the idiom means losing one's temper all at once.

a.note: Slipping away quietly is the opposite of the loud outburst a blown fuse suggests.

b.note: Vanishing suddenly takes 'blow' to mean 'disappear'; a blown fuse is an outburst, not a disappearance.

d.note: Managing a situation smartly has nothing to do with losing control.

pyqs.trick: A blown fuse is an electrical outburst: sudden anger.

'on thin ice'
options: In a risky position where things could go wrong
Not very sensible or intelligent
Something that will never happen
To argue against an idea only to test it
practice.why: 'on thin ice' means: in a risky position where things could go wrong.

b.note: That is the meaning of 'not playing with a full deck', not of 'on thin ice'.

c.note: That is the meaning of 'when pigs fly', not of 'on thin ice'.

d.note: That is the meaning of 'play devil's advocate', not of 'on thin ice'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
'a penny for your thoughts'
options: To tell only the main point, briefly
A way of asking what someone is thinking
To spoil someone's pleasure or plans
To judge something by its looks alone
practice.why: 'a penny for your thoughts' means: a way of asking what someone is thinking.

a.note: That is the meaning of 'make a long story short', not of 'a penny for your thoughts'.

c.note: That is the meaning of 'rain on someone's parade', not of 'a penny for your thoughts'.

d.note: That is the meaning of 'judge a book by its cover', not of 'a penny for your thoughts'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
'quick on the draw'
options: To risk everything on a single plan
Something that will never happen
Quick to react or reply
To argue against an idea only to test it
practice.why: 'quick on the draw' means: quick to react or reply.

a.note: That is the meaning of 'put all one's eggs in one basket', not of 'quick on the draw'.

b.note: That is the meaning of 'when pigs fly', not of 'quick on the draw'.

d.note: That is the meaning of 'play devil's advocate', not of 'quick on the draw'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
'rain or shine'
options: Feeling sad or depressed
In a difficult situation
Not very sensible or intelligent
In any weather; whatever happens
practice.why: 'rain or shine' means: in any weather; whatever happens.

a.note: That is the meaning of 'down in the dumps', not of 'rain or shine'.

b.note: That is the meaning of 'in a pickle', not of 'rain or shine'.

c.note: That is the meaning of 'not playing with a full deck', not of 'rain or shine'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
'see eye to eye'
options: To agree completely
To make a mistake about whom or what to blame or pursue
To start something quickly and with energy
To make every possible effort to achieve a goal
practice.why: 'see eye to eye' means: to agree completely.

b.note: That is the meaning of 'bark up the wrong tree', not of 'see eye to eye'.

c.note: That is the meaning of 'hit the ground running', not of 'see eye to eye'.

d.note: That is the meaning of 'leave no stone unturned', not of 'see eye to eye'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
'up the creek without a paddle'
options: To get absorbed in a deep and confusing subject
In a difficult situation with no way out
Perfectly neat and tidy
Follow the customs of the place you are in
practice.why: 'up the creek without a paddle' means: in a difficult situation with no way out.

a.note: That is the meaning of 'go down the rabbit hole', not of 'up the creek without a paddle'.

c.note: That is the meaning of 'not a hair out of place', not of 'up the creek without a paddle'.

d.note: That is the meaning of 'when in Rome, do as the Romans do', not of 'up the creek without a paddle'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
'when in Rome, do as the Romans do'
options: To argue against an idea only to test it
A person who can do many different jobs
Follow the customs of the place you are in
To stop a problem at an early stage
practice.why: 'when in Rome, do as the Romans do' means: follow the customs of the place you are in.

a.note: That is the meaning of 'play devil's advocate', not of 'when in Rome, do as the Romans do'.

b.note: That is the meaning of 'a jack of all trades', not of 'when in Rome, do as the Romans do'.

d.note: That is the meaning of 'nip in the bud', not of 'when in Rome, do as the Romans do'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
'year in, year out'
options: To stay cheerful in hard times
To decide what to do as events unfold, without a plan
Available for anyone to take or win
Every year, without a break
practice.why: 'year in, year out' means: every year, without a break.

a.note: That is the meaning of 'keep one's chin up', not of 'year in, year out'.

b.note: That is the meaning of 'play it by ear', not of 'year in, year out'.

c.note: That is the meaning of 'up for grabs', not of 'year in, year out'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
'at sixes and sevens'
options: In a state of confusion or disorder
Great things take time and patience
Help each other by exchanging favours
Those who act early gain the advantage
practice.why: 'at sixes and sevens' means: in a state of confusion or disorder.

b.note: That is the meaning of 'Rome was not built in a day', not of 'at sixes and sevens'.

c.note: That is the meaning of 'you scratch my back and I will scratch yours', not of 'at sixes and sevens'.

d.note: That is the meaning of 'the early bird catches the worm', not of 'at sixes and sevens'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
'blow a fuse'
options: A way of asking what someone is thinking
To lose one's temper suddenly
Follow the customs of the place you are in
To lose hope or confidence
practice.why: 'blow a fuse' means: to lose one's temper suddenly.

a.note: That is the meaning of 'a penny for your thoughts', not of 'blow a fuse'.

c.note: That is the meaning of 'when in Rome, do as the Romans do', not of 'blow a fuse'.

d.note: That is the meaning of 'lose heart', not of 'blow a fuse'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
'shoulder the responsibility'
options: To reveal a secret
To avoid coming to the main point
To accept a duty or blame as one's own
To become impossible to control
practice.why: 'shoulder the responsibility' means: to accept a duty or blame as one's own.

a.note: That is the meaning of 'spill the beans', not of 'shoulder the responsibility'.

b.note: That is the meaning of 'beat around the bush', not of 'shoulder the responsibility'.

d.note: That is the meaning of 'get out of hand', not of 'shoulder the responsibility'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
'at cross purposes'
options: Very rarely
Something very easy to do
Feeling slightly unwell
Misunderstanding each other's aims
practice.why: 'at cross purposes' means: misunderstanding each other's aims.

a.note: That is the meaning of 'once in a blue moon', not of 'at cross purposes'.

b.note: That is the meaning of 'a piece of cake', not of 'at cross purposes'.

c.note: That is the meaning of 'under the weather', not of 'at cross purposes'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
'lose heart'
options: To lose hope or confidence
To be upset about a loss that cannot be undone
While overcome by strong feeling and without thinking
Nothing worthwhile is achieved without effort
practice.why: 'lose heart' means: to lose hope or confidence.

b.note: That is the meaning of 'cry over spilt milk', not of 'lose heart'.

c.note: That is the meaning of 'in the heat of the moment', not of 'lose heart'.

d.note: That is the meaning of 'no pain, no gain', not of 'lose heart'.

practice.text:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
'have a chip on one's shoulder'
options: To keep something dangerous or unwelcome away
To feel angry or resentful about a past wrong
To postpone something for later
To show one's feelings openly
practice.why: 'have a chip on one's shoulder' means: to feel angry or resentful about a past wrong.

a.note: That is the meaning of 'keep at bay', not of 'have a chip on one's shoulder'.

c.note: That is the meaning of 'put on ice', not of 'have a chip on one's shoulder'.

d.note: That is the meaning of 'wear one's heart on one's sleeve', not of 'have a chip on one's shoulder'.
